newsitem.title: USA: Study says US farm income to be boosted by ethanol.
newsitem.headline: Study says US farm income to be boosted by ethanol.

text.p: Ethanol production is expected to boost farmers' incomes in the United States, according to a new economic study.

U.S. net farm income will increase this year by $4.5 billion as a result of ethanol demand, said the author of the report, Michael Evans, professor of economics at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management.
"The increase in farm income has come from higher corn prices," Evans told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Ethanol, a gasoline additive made from corn, reduces harmful emissions such as carbon monoxide and ozone.

"So far we have determined that corn prices will be 45 cents per bushel higher in 1997 than would have been the case if ethanol demand were zero," Evans wrote in his economic study, titled "The Economic Impact of the Demand for Ethanol".
Evans also pegged this year's corn production at 9.1 billion bushels. Evans said total cash receipts from corn for the 1996/97 year are expected to be 9.14 billion times $2.75 or $25.1 billion.
"If the demand for ethanol were zero, we estimate that crop production would be 8.72 billion bushels, and the average price would be $2.30," Evans said.
In that case, total cash receipts from corn would be $20.1 billion. "Thus gross cash receipts to corn growers are $5.0 billion higher because of the demand for ethanol," Evans said.

The study estimated more ethanol production this year compared with 1996, when ethanol production dropped sharply as a result of lower corn output. "We think this will be a good year for corn production," Evans said.
"It is assumed that ethanol production will get back to its trend rate in 1997, which is about 1.5 billion gallons or equivalent to about 600 million bushels of corn," Evans said.
The Evans study also validated the federal ethanol program.

"There was a lot of talk about eliminating the tax credit for ethanol. I thought somebody had to point out there are actually some benefits to this tax credit because farm income growth is up and we import less oil, so oil prices go down," Evans said.
"I think it would benefit the taxpayer because it would keep the price of oil down," he said.

Eric Vaughn, president of the Renewable Fuels Association said the tax incentive of 5.4 cents per gallon goes to gasoline marketers and blenders and was initiated to make ethanol a more viable and competitive octane enhancer and fuel oxygenate in gasoline.
The excise tax incentive is due to expire in the year 2000. But several congressmen have introduced a bill to end the ethanol incentive in two years instead of 2000.
The Evans study was sponsored by the Midwestern Governors' Conference, an association of governors from 12 U.S. states.
